Telemachus. The son of Odysseus and Penelope, introduced in Homer's Odyssey as a young man on the threshold of adulthood. While his father endures a decade-long journey home from Troy, Telemachus grows up in his absence, harassed by suitors consuming his inheritance and pressuring his mother to remarry. His own journey of self-discovery, seeking news of his father and reclaiming his inheritance, parallels Odysseus's voyage and emphasizes the costs of war on the next generation.

He was an infant, mere weeks or months old, when Odysseus left for the Trojan War. He is a young man of approximately twenty when the Odyssey begins, knowing his father only through stories and legend. He is tormented by his mother's increasingly aggressive suitors, who occupy his father's palace, consume his family's livestock and resources, and publicly demand she choose one of them to marry.

He lacks the authority to expel the suitors despite being the nominal prince. His youth and uncertain paternity, some suitors claim Odysseus died at Troy, undermine his legitimacy. Inspired by the goddess Athena, disguised as Mentes, he departs Ithaca to seek news of his father. He travels first to Pylos to consult the elderly king Nestor, then to Sparta to visit Menelaus.

He learns from these encounters that Odysseus is alive and that the goddess Calypso holds him captive on an island. Crucial knowledge that transforms his understanding of his duty and heritage. He returns to Ithaca just as Odysseus arrives in disguise, and together they orchestrate the slaughter of the suitors in a bloody climax. Telemachus fights alongside his father as a man come of age.

He participates actively in the massacre of the suitors, asserting his rightful claim to his father's throne, inheritance, and dignity, and finally becoming the adult prince he could not be in his father's absence. In some later accounts, post-Homeric, he becomes a founder of new cities or marries Circe's daughter Cassiope, extending the Odyssey's narrative beyond Homer's text.

Odysseus is his father, whose absence defines his coming-of-age and whose return requires his aid. Penelope is his mother, whose loyalty and need to choose a husband creates his crisis. The Odyssey is the epic in which his parallel journey structures much of the narrative. Ithaca is his home and the inheritance he fights to reclaim. Athena is the goddess who guides his journey and supports his maturation. The suitors of Penelope are the antagonists who threaten his inheritance and his mother's choice.
